utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody and let me start off by apologising for the late start of the case this morning. It's all because of my problems and they were all beyond my control, but I hope I'm forgiven for that. Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have the appearances for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Laurie Sartorio. We are assisted today by our intern, Sarai Jacob, and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Witness, can I remind you that, although you may be aware of it, it is my duty to do so, that you are bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. So you must continue doing so even today. Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the record, on behalf of Mr. Delic's Defence, Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson with assistants, Lana Deljkic and Asja Zujo. I apologise .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must apologise. I am very sorry. Thank you so much, Madam Vidovic. Okay, Mr. Robson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, I'd like to briefly recap on the evidence you gave yesterday. You told us that following the attack on Maline village, you travelled in a group of Bosnian Croats towards the village of Mehurici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And that group you were in was escorted by three or four Bosnian army soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: After you passed the village of Poljanice, you noticed another group of about 15 Bosnian Croat men travelling along in the opposite direction; is that so?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, that group of Bosnian Croat men was escorted by two foreign and two local Mujahedin; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The local Mujahedin had green masks covering their faces, and those Mujahedin stopped your group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And those Mujahedin used force to separate you and the other Bosnian Croat men in your group, and they pushed you together with the other -- with the Bosnian Croat men in the other group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, after the Mujahedin separated the men from the group that you were originally in, that original group continued on its way in the direction of Mehurici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first group that had to return had been moving in the direction of Bikosi and Poljanice. Those were Bosnian Croats. They had to go back. I was in the second group. However, a group of civilians was joined to the first group of Croats who had to go back towards Poljanice and Bikosi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the group of civilians that you mentioned, so that group contained your wife and children, that group continued on its way towards Mehurici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So after you were separated and put into the new group of Bosnian Croat men, you continued in the direction of Maline and you were escorted by these Mujahedin; is that so?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were escorted, but we were moving in the direction of Poljanice. Poljanice came first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you told us how, as that group continued along, you met with other people; you mentioned a female, Ana Pranjes, and some wounded Bosnian Croats as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We came across these people in the village of Poljanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, at this stage, I would like to clarify something that you told us in your evidence. You referred to some of the men that carried out the separation of the Bosnian Croats as being members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, and, indeed, that was the case. They had the insignia on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to go into private session at this stage, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, I want to show you another document that was provided to the Defence by the Prosecution. This is a statement that was given to the Commission for the Verification of War Crimes on the Territory of Croatia -- of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Do you remember me asking you about this commission yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, have you had a chance to think, do you remember giving a statement to that commission?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that I was in Medjugorje? That it was from Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This commission was in Mostar or certainly based in Mostar. Whether the statement was given in Mostar or someone else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Mostar. As far as the statement is concerned, I can hardly remember whether I gave it or not. I cannot say. I did give several local statements. I cannot remember them all. I just remember just this which I gave in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Before we look at the document, I'd just like to check with you that the commission spoke with someone who gave his name as Berislav Marijanovic, who had a father named Nikola. Is your father called Nikola?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the person they spoke to was born on the 27th of February 1966. Is that your birthday?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the person they spoke to lived in or was from Paklarevo in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And that's where you're from, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could look at this document, please, it's Defence document D105. Okay. The particular pages that I'm interested in, it's page 4 in the English version and page 3 in the B/C/S version. Now, in the English version at page 4, we are interested in the second half of that document, the part that begins, "That unit was Muslim," and there after.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, if you could look at page 3 of the B/C/S version, it's the second paragraph, towards the top of that page. Now, do you see in that document, Mr. Marijanovic, where the person is --

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the person is explaining to the members of the commission about the people that carried out the shooting in Bikosi, and what it states is: "That unit was Muslim, that Jihad of theirs; some other Igba, whatever. That was some Muslim unit of theirs; the names were changing. Those who were escorting us and shooting at us - there were about seven of them; I do not remember exactly, I was confused - I cannot tell how many there were exactly. "At the points of execution, some more joined them, but there were seven who had been escorting us. Of the seven, four were Mujahedins and three were local people. I knew it by their accents and behaviour and such. These local people had stockings on their heads." Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you accept that the members of the commission must have spoken to you to get that information and record it in the document?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I agree that those people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, the question just to clarify that is that the members of the commission must have spoken to you to get that information and to record that in the document. They wouldn't have been able to --

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, when you were interviewed by that commission, no mention was made to them that members of the Bosnian army carried out the shooting, was there?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who else it was, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You were very specific, weren't you, when you gave that information. You said it was a Muslim unit with a name, some Jihad of theirs, whatever.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look here, the Muslim army, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what shall I call it, it wasn't the Serbs. It wasn't any other army. I don't know what else to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If members of the Bosnian army had been carrying out the killings in Bikosi that day, you would have told the members of that commission, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we call them the Muslim army, the Croat army, and the Serb army. That's what we the locals called them; and according to that, I gave my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Marijanovic. I have no further questions, and I've certainly no desire to take you through the events of Bikosi again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. Any re-examination, Ms. Sartorio?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We have no redirect, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, thank you very much for coming to testify. The Trial Chamber wants to thank you for taking the time off your busy schedule to come and testify. That brings us to the end of your testimony. You are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before we call the next witness, there had been an exchange of correspondence, yesterday, concerning a witness who is scheduled to appear from Tuesday through Thursday of next week, and I believe that Mrs. Vidovic had come comments with respect to the proposed procedure that the Prosecution put forward in its letter to the Defence yesterday. And I believe that she wanted to address the Trial Chamber on that point before the next witness is called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just before -- sorry to interrupt. But this witness was the subject of protective measures in a prior case, so I think we can deal with this in open session as long as the witness's name is not mentioned. If the Chamber has the calendar, he's the witness scheduled for Tuesday through Thursday of next week. We can do this in open session as long as everyone is cognizant of the fact that he did testify with a pseudonym in this prior case, and, of course, Rule 75(F) would indicate that those protective measures carry over into these proceedings in the absence of an order rescinding or varying those protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. This is the one who is testifying from Tuesday next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, and when that -- I should also say, when that calendar was produced, we were unaware that the Chamber would not sit on Friday, the 27th. We are certainly aware of that at this point, but that would explain why the calendar has us going Tuesday to Friday with this witness, when in fact it's Tuesday to Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. We understand. Now I know who you're talking about. Madam Vidovic are you able to talk about this topic in open session and without endangering any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are able. I am able, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as my colleague, Mr. Mundis, has said, it was yesterday that we received the proposal in a correspondence, in a letter from the Prosecutor, in which he demanded that, in keeping with Article 92 ter, the interviews, seven interviews of this witness be admitted into the case file, including, I believe, also the -- and the audio interview of this witness, about which I talked at the Pre-Trial Conference. Your Honours, we had occasion to discuss this in several instances yesterday, and we do have a problem that we are wholly unable to overcome; namely, we are far advanced in our cross-examination and I have already said that this is a very complex testimony, so that the cross-examination is actually being prepared on the basis of the statement of that witness given in this case, in the case against General Delic. The other statements are very voluminous. It is at least 650 pages of court transcripts, 12 hours of this interview, and over 60 pages of other interviews. Your Honours, I have certainly read and perused and I always very carefully read the previously given statements, but it is not just a matter of reading those statements. It is also a matter of something else, at least that is how I proceed in preparing my cross-examination, which is to analyse the evidence given in the testimony of the witness. There is no possibility whatsoever for me, in so short a time, to prepare my cross-examination in respect of the other seven statements; and with your permission, believe me, that I -- I believe that nobody else would be able to do so. I had a very short time in which to prepare myself. The transcript lasts for 12 and a half -- about 12 and a half hours. I received it only two weeks ago. So it takes a great effort on my part to prepare my cross-examination on the basis of a transcript of that length received only two weeks ago. Believe me, Your Honours, I would be unable to proceed with my cross-examination on that basis. I'm sure that the Prosecutor believes that he has saved time required for the examination-in-chief. However, even if I had known a month before about his intention to have these transcripts admitted into case file, I would certainly require three times as much time to prepare for the cross-examination, so that I believe that this would not even be warranted by court economy considerations. I certainly will have to deal with all the parts of the earlier-given statements and interviews. That is why I can embark on the cross-examination of this witness only if the basis for it is the statement against my client given in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I've heard your argument. What are you objecting to? What are you asking for? Just in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My purpose, actually, the Prosecutor did not address a motion to the Trial Chamber. What I am asking is that the earlier given statements of this witness not be admitted into the case file, and that the cross-examination -- that the examination of the witness continue on Tuesday, but on the basis of his statement given in this case. What I'm opposing is the admission of his statements made in accordance with Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. It is time to take the break. Can I suggest that we take the break and continue with this discussion when we come back? Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. We will take a break now and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, just why do we want this witness to complete his testimony before recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will answer that question; and then if there are any remaining questions, my colleague, Ms. Sartorio, will be dealing with the witness. But the bottom line is, Your Honours, in order to -- we proposed this in order to save time, and so the witness can complete his testimony prior to the recess, both for the convenience of the sake of the witness, but also because of the fact that with the time constraints that we all operate under here at the Tribunal, we believe that this witness's testimony can be completed in three complete court days, if the specific provisions of Rule 92 ter are applied with respect to part of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But it appears as if to both the Prosecution and the Defence, this is a very important witness, and do the considerations of justice and fair trial not outweigh the considerations of expeditiousness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. And if I had 150 or 200 hours of direct examination to put on my case, we would probably conduct a more extensive and lengthy direct examination of this witness. But all of the trials before this Tribunal, we need to take into consideration all of these various factors; and as a result of that, we have decided on the OTP side to reduce the amount of time we spend with this witness, so that we can present the fullest possible case to the Trial Chamber in the amount of time available to us. And as a result of that, I believe this witness was initially scheduled for six hours of direct examination. We have reduced that to three hours, while at the same time preserving, in our respectful views, adequate time for the Defence to cross-examine the witness and for any questions that might arise to be handled on redirect, and, of course, to preserve as much time as possible for questions from the Bench. This is why we have proposed this procedure, a variation, if you will, of Rule 92 ter, which specifically allows that the evidence may be heard in whole or in part by way of writing. This witness has testified previously. He has testified on some of the same exact matters that are relevant to this case, and, again, the witness was cross-examined on those issues. The witness was questioned by the Trial Chamber in the previous case on these issues, and we believe given the overall time limit that is three days, rather than the initially scheduled four, would be adequate in light of the overall constraints, if we are permitted to use Rule 92 ter to adduce some of his evidence by way of that rule and the specific provisions therein. And, of course, we do have a number of documents to deal with the witness as well, so we can't just do a 92 ter procedure with him. We would need to ask him some questions to highlight some of his prior testimony or prior information in prior statements, but -- and to show him some documents. But we do believe, given the overall constraints that everyone - and I'm not just talking about the Prosecution, but I'm talking about the Defence and the Chamber as well - within these overall constraints, we believe that we can adequately examine this witness in three hours of direct examination, which would be in effect one court day or slightly less than one court day, which would then leave two days for cross-examination, redirect, and any questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't want you to misunderstand the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber appreciates very much what you suggest in terms of saving time. At the same time, the Trial Chamber would like to be -- show that the trial is fair to the accused. And as expeditious as we would like to go, we would also like to make sure that we don't compromise fairness. And my question would then be: In the likely event that the Defence is not able to cross-examine this witness and finish with their cross-examination before we go for recess, and the witness has to come back, to what extent would that be an inconvenience to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would not be a major inconvenience. I, at one point, earlier this week or perhaps it was late last week, spoke about this issue with the Defence. And I don't want to put words in my learned colleague's mouth, but my understanding at that time was that the Defence would also prefer not to have a split between either the direct and the cross or to have the cross broken in two, in effect. I have already provided and we've arranged for witnesses for the following two weeks, or the last two weeks in August. The witness could probably be scheduled to return in mid-September to complete any cross-examination that may not be completed. But we would also indicate that because the witness was previously cross-examined on many of these same issues, that the cross-examination might not be as lengthy on those issues as would otherwise be the case, if it were to be a completely viva voce direct examination; that is, if the Trial Chamber has the transcripts of the prior testimony of the witness, obviously, that would include the prior cross-examination as well. I don't have at this point an indication from the Defence as to the amount of time they think they would need for the cross-examination of this witness, so I don't want to comment on that; and, of course, it also depends on the content of the direct examination and the witness's comments with respect to the number of documents that we would be showing him and tendering through him. So it's a bit premature or hard for me to gauge whether it would be possible for the Defence to complete their cross-examination in the roughly two days or day and a half of court time that would be available to them. It would not be -- I will state this, though: It will not be a major inconvenience to the Prosecution if the witness had to come back in mid-September. It very well might be a major inconvenience for the witness, and that might not be the course of action which the Defence would prefer; but, again, we believe that the amount of time available is adequate to deal with this witness, as I've indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Finally, if the Prosecution, in its 92 ter procedure, were to highlight and condense the documents that are to be put through this witness to a much lesser figure than the 650 pages that are being mentioned, would that facilitate the leading of this witness within the space of time that you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could just make some general comments on that very issue, because I think it's important for the overall running of the entire trial, including, of course, the Defence case, if there is to be one, following the 98 bis phase, I would then turn to Ms. Sartorio with respects to the specifics of this witness. But if I could just make some general comments on this, the Trial Chamber is undoubtedly aware that, in the Prosecution's comments on the proposed trial guidelines, we noted that the use of 92 ter was not specifically addressed in those proposed trial guidelines, and we specifically asked for some guidance on this very issue. It would be possible for the Prosecution to reduce those transcripts, in effect, into a new 92 ter statement. The problem with that would be that such a statement would probably be produced to the Defence on Monday afternoon, immediately prior to us then coming in on Tuesday and conducting the direct examination. And I say that because the witness will be proofed on Sunday and Monday morning, and it's unlikely that we would be in a position to produce a statement condensing that material until shortly before the witness appeared, and that might create other problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I probably misspoke. What I'm thinking of is that the Prosecution deals with the witness not as a 92 ter witness, but as an ordinary 65 ter witness, and in leading him, concentrate on those parts of the 650 pages that are so important to the Prosecution, that, in fact, the 650 can then get reduced to a much lesser number, and then hand over the witness to the Defence to cross-examine and let them take whatever time they take. And if it means that the witness has to come back after recess, so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, having consulted with Ms. Sartorio, who, as I've indicated, will be leading the witness, it would be possible to do that. However, that will require six hours of direct examination, with the result that the witness obviously would have to come back for cross-examination; and then the issue becomes whether the Defence starts the cross-examination or whether the cross-examination simply extends over, and we would then schedule the witness to return at some point probably in mid-September for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The reason I'm asking you is this is because you say, in this letter to Madam Vidovic, that the purpose of this limited examination is to focus the Chamber on those portions of (redacted). And I think that the fairness of the trial weighs heavier on the scale; and if the witness has to come back, so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I completely understand and agree that, obviously, there might be situations where witnesses have to return for cross-examination, and this witness very well may fall into that category. What I am concerned about is, of course, the fairness, as the Trial Chamber rightly is, with respect to the fairness of the accused to a fair trial. We, of course, submit that the Prosecution is also entitled to a fair trial in terms of the amount of time that we have available. The Chamber is well aware that this issue has been raised before, and will continue, I would suggest, to be an issue until such time as there is a ruling on the pending 73 bis (F) application. Those numbers and figures that we proposed in the annex, annex A, to that filing, clearly anticipated three hour direct examination for this witness, because we were in the process of developing and thinking about how to streamline this procedure. So, again, our concerns will be that if it takes us six hours instead of three, that that would result in us being squeezed later down the road, and I want to, again, just simply put that on the record. Of course, we will proceed in whichever way the Trial Chamber directs us to proceed, but I do want to at least put our concerns on the record with respect to what I think will continue to be time pressures on all of the parties or both of the parties to this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, I hear your argument, and I have every sympathy for that argument. Given the importance that everybody seems to attach to this witness, I would rather suggest that if it has to take the Prosecution six hours to lead the witness, so be it, and the decision on the 73 bis (F) will take into account that problem. And let's deal with this witness as thoroughly as we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Would that be okay with you, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, absolutely. Let the Prosecutor use the six hours that he envisaged. What is important for us is that we get enough time for cross-examination and enough time to prepare the witness; and in that case, we are totally agreeable with the Trial Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam. So it's decided. Mr. Mundis, call your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prosecution calls Zdravko Pranjes, and my colleague, Mr. Menon, will be leading this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may be seated, sir. Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pranjes.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name, and your place of birth for the record?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: My name is Zdravko Pranjes. I was born in Travnik on the 12th of July 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Where were you raised, Mr. Pranjes?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: The village of Maline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you please describe the ethnic composition of Maline?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: The village of Maline is part Muslim. That's Lower or Donje Maline, and we Croats lived in Gornje or Upper Maline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, were you ever a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: When did you join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And was there a particular brigade or unit that you joined?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Frankopan Brigade, that's the one I joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where was this unit based?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: It was based in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, you mentioned that you were raised in the village of Maline. In the spring of 1993, was this village your home?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes. I had a home there. That's where I resided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in that time period, how was the -- how would you describe the relationship between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats in the area around Maline and in Maline?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Well, the situation was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did -- I'm speaking about the spring of 1993. Did the relationship deteriorate at any point?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes. It deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you describe how it deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: There were some incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you describe -- can you describe these incidents?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: It was a Thursday, and we were going to the market in Travnik, my father and me, and a cousin and his wife. In the morning on our way to town, everything was normal, just like every day. But on our way back, when we entered towards Guca Gora, we saw a crowd of people looking at something on the road. We didn't ask what was going on, but went on; and when we got to Gornje Maline, they filed shots at us, at our car, from Donje Maline. Only -- it was only when we got to the village that I saw the car had been hit; and since that time, the situation became tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: What, if any, steps did you and the other -- did you and the other villagers in Maline and the surrounding villages take to protect these villages, the Bosnian Croat villages?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: We set up guards around the village and up on the hill where our line was. We strengthened the measures. We were more alert. We were more careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you describe -- can you indicate where your line was? Which places are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Between the houses in the village, about 100 metres away from the houses, and then up along Greda down to Suhi Dol and Mekuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask if the witness could be shown map -- the electronic version of map 9 from the map book. It's the ERN is 0618-6704. And I'm going to have the witness make some markings on this, so if the usher could assist him with that. Can you please scroll down? Yes. That's good. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, can you see the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you please use the pen that's being handed to you to draw a line where the positions that you've just indicated were? And I'm speaking about the defensive positions that you said had been put in place to protects the villagers.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I'm going to have --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Pranjes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm going to have the witness make one more marking on this, so if it could just remain on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, was your village, the village of Gornje Maline, was that ever attacked?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: No, but they fired shots from time to time. On the day before last, they fired shots on the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say, "day before last," which time period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: It was on the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: 7th of June. And I want to take you to the 8th of June. Was there ever -- was there an attack against your village on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Then, at 5.00 in the morning, the village was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you said "5.00 in the morning." What day are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: The 8th of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who was responsible for this attack?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I don't know who was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you know which forces attacked that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes. They were Muslim forces. We know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when this attack occurred, where were you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I was at Greda where I had been deployed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to have you make a marking on the map in front of you. If you could take the -- if you could do that with the blue pen. And you indicated that you were at Greda, so if you could mark with an "X" the location of Greda?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask this if exhibit could be tendered into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Prosecutor, I would like to understand better the significance of the red line drawn by the witness. Was this a front line, and did they have trenches along those lines? Or was it just an area which they patrolled or was it moved subsequently, or what is actually the significance of the line? I didn't quite understand from the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, you heard the question of the Judge. What was the significance of this line -- of the line that you've marked with the red? What was the reason for having established this line?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: We had our trenches there. We had our trenches there because we were afraid we might be attacked, so that's where we stood guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: So was this -- this was a defensive line, then, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if the lines with the trenches were manned by HVO soldiers at all during this time, at least in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was only us villagers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking is that if someone were to cross your lines, say from walking from the north towards the south, would he then necessarily encounter any of your troops when crossing this line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Donje Maline, they would go there to guard sheep, but the guards were set up in order to prevent soldiers from opening fire at us. If fire was opened, then we would return it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also have a question with regard to this line. You said that the Croats, the inhabitants of the villages, Maline, lived in the upper part of Maline, Gornje Maline. So I don't quite understand why the defence line crosses the village, dividing it in two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because the Muslims opened fire at us. How else could we have made the line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why not below or under Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because this is Gornje Maline and this is Donje Maline. I don't know exactly where the border between the two is, but I suppose that the border would be here, somewhere about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So perhaps it's just a question of the way you drew the line. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, what divides Upper Maline, Gornje Maline, from Lower Maline? Is there some kind of a structure or marking or territory?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: There is nothing to divide the two. There were a few houses mixed. There were some Muslim houses mixed with Croatian houses, and there was a little path; otherwise, there was no clear division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you had said that you were deployed at Greda. Do you remember the names of the other people who were deployed at Greda with you --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: -- and if so, can you please indicate their names?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Jako Tavic was one of them. There was also Franjo Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And in response to the attack that took place, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: We opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And then did you continue to fire at the forces that were attacking you, or did you -- or was there something else that you did?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: We were opening fire for as long as we could, but then we realised that we had been encircled. In Lazine, they started opening fire from the houses, some houses were set fire to, and that's when we withdrew. We went down to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And was there a particular location that you retreated to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I retreated to my own house; actually, to my relative's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And was this in the village of Maline -- Gornje Maline? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, in Gornje Maline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you said you retreated to your relative's house. What was the name of your relative?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Ivo Pranjes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the map on which the witness made some markings be tendered into evidence. It's still on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And Mr. Ivo Pranjes's house, was it being used for some kind of a purpose; and if so, what purpose was it being used for?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: It was used as a makeshift hospital for people who were wounded; and Ivo himself, he occupied the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you go inside this makeshift hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes. I was there, and I took the body of a woman who had been killed into the house, together with Jako.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And so when you went in the house, the attack that had been -- that had been waged against the village, it was continuing, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you explain how that attack came to an end?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They wanted to negotiate. Two women went to negotiate: Ljubica Djakovic and Kata Blazevic. They returned shortly after, and they told us that we were supposed to surrender our weapons. We did that. Ljubica and Kata took the weapons over there. The Muslims, or at least some of them, had already descended behind the houses. The Muslim army came with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you explain who Ljubica Djakovic and Kata Blazevic were?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Ljubica was a nurse, and Kata was helping her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where were they when these calls for surrender had come?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They were in this hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. And you had indicated that -- you'd made reference in your earlier answer to the Muslim army. How did you know that this was a Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: On that day, we had heard -- actually, we realised what the direction they had come from. We knew where they would be taking us. We could tell by the clothes, and we knew from what people told us. I believe this is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you said -- you stated that the -- well, let me rephrase that. When the Muslim army came into the village, where were you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: In front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. And, among the soldiers that came to where you were, was there one that was in charge?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: There was a blond, young man. He had been wounded. There was blood on his head, and his wounds were dressed with a piece of white cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you describe the appearance of the other soldiers that were around the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They wore green uniforms. They looked like regular troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And the soldier that was in charge did he order you and the others who were at the hospital, did he order you to do anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just concerned that you were likely going to put words into the mouth of the witness, and I just wanted you to rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sure. I apologise for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The soldier that was in charge, what, if anything, did he order the people who were around the hospital to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you should ask the witness what happened next, and then he can tell you if any ordering was made at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, after you had gathered outside the hospital, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: We brought a woman who had been wounded during the attack. The woman was pregnant. We took her in front of Stipe Jacovic's house. That's where she was wounded, and then we took her to the hospital from there. Later on, they asked whose car it was in the garage. They asked me to give them the key. Actually, I was the one who was told to drive it out of the garage; then they took the key from me, and then they took the key to my relative's lorry, and then they said that the women should take the bear necessities from their houses, that we should release the cattle from the cow sheds, and that we should start walking to join the column of Croats around Travnik. And that column was moving towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, you keep saying "they ordered me to give them the key." Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you referred to a car begin taken --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Did Your Honours have a question? I thought I heard something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Were there other incidents where vehicles were taken from the village?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Well, yes. My relative's truck was driven away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you mentioned this column that was moving towards Mehurici. How many people were in that column?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: About 300 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you reach Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Why didn't you reach Mehurici? What happened?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Before we entered Mehuric, we were jumped by the Mujahedin. There were some other armed men with them. They jumped in front of the column. They separated the able-bodied Croats, and they told us to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by "Mujahedin"? Can you describe the physical appearance of these people?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They were dark-skinned. They sported long beards. I had never seen them before that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how many -- how many Mujahedin were there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Maybe four or five, and there were also those with hats on their faces with just slots for their eyes and their mouth. They were wearing that kind of masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, in terms of these people that you refer to who were wearing "hats on their faces," how many such people were there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Maybe four or five in the part where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did the one -- and did both groups appear at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. But the others were maybe ten or 15 metres away, but I would say that they appeared more or less at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where exactly did they appear from? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Those that I saw appeared from a meadow, and there is a hedge around that meadow. We were walking by that meadow. They jumped out of the meadow, which was partly fenced off, partly separated from us by that hedge, and that's where they jumped from and landed right in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And with respect -- and you had described the Mujahedin as being dark-skinned and sporting long beards. Was that the first time that day that you had seen such people who had fit this type of description?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown map 10 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. There was one in the village who was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And which village are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: The village of Maline, actually a hamlet called Tavici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where in relation to Maline is the hamlet of Tavici?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Why do we call Tavici? For example, Celo Maline -- actually, we call Tavici because it is inhabited by people who share that same family name, Tavici. Where I hail from is the village of Pranjesi. And down there where the Jurici is, that's where the family Jurici lived. And all these places were next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: So Tavici would be next to Maline, is that it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: In Maline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: In Maline?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: It's a whole village, but there are different family names, and there was the Tavici family that lived in some five or six houses in that part of the village that we then referred to as the hamlet of Tavici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown map 10, Your Honour, the electronic version of that map, and I'm going to have him -- it's on the screen. Okay. And if we could somehow get the whole map on to the screen at the same time? Okay. And I'm going to have him make some markings so if the usher could assist him again? The whole map, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very difficult for me to determine exactly and see whether this is a road or not. That's why it's very difficult. That's why I made the mistake before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, I still need to ask you the question actually. I think you're anticipating what I want to ask you. What I wanted you to do is, to the best of your recollection, mark the path that you took from Gornje Maline to the point where you were separated from the column that was moving towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, yes. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you mark, with the number 1, the point at which you were separated, and draw a circle around the 1.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm going to have him make a few more markings on that map, so if that could remain on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, the people who separated you from the column, did you hear any of them speak?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I did hear them, but I did not understand them, those that sported the beards, the Mujahedin. I also heard the others with the hats on their heads, but I could understand them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what language were the people that were wearing hats, what language were they speaking?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you happen to notice how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I don't know whether they had green uniforms or some other coloured uniforms. I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. And how many people were separated from the column that was moving towards Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Maybe 30 or 40, in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you name some of the people who were separated, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Jako Pranjes was one of them; Jako Tavic; his brother, Mijo Tavic; Slavko Kramar; Bero Marijanovic; Juric, Ivo was his name. Just a moment. His son as well, I can't remember his name; then there was Ana Pranjes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: There were others, but I can't remember all of them. And there were a lot of people from Podstinje from Pode, whose names I didn't know then, and I don't know them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And were the Mujahedin and the others who separated you from the group that was going towards Mehurici, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you describe how they went about separating these people? How did they accomplish that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They simply jumped. They pointed their guns at us. They shouted. I don't know what. One of them singled out somebody from the column -- actually, he wanted to single him out, and the soldier grabbed that person and returned him to the column. Then the first man started shouting at the soldier, threatening him or something. The whole column came to a halt. They were walking up and down, and then more Mujahedin came down there. And I suppose that they had forced the others to separate us from the others. The commander -- actually, the one that I thought was the commander, who had been the first to arrive in the village, he was shouting, "Command, command." I suppose that he was forced to do this. I don't know exactly, but I only know that eventually we were separated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon, how much longer are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Another ten to 15 minutes, Your Honour, not long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have gone beyond an hour. You estimated 45 minutes for your testimony .

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm told we started at 11.03, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We did. You are virtually there, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. I will speed it up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pranjes, the people who were not separated, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They were taken to Mehurici. As for afterwards, what happened to them, I didn't know. They were taken down there to the village of Mehurici, and we were taken back to Bikosi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And within this column that was moving towards Bikosi, where were you positioned?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I was at the front end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who was standing next to you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Jako Tavic was by my side all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you were moving to -- that this column was going towards Bikosi. Did you encounter anyone -- did you encounter anyone else en route to Bikosi, any other people?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: There were the wounded people from our hospital in Maline up above Poljanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where did you -- up above Poljanice. Okay. Thank you. And how many people were there? How many wounded did you encounter?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did any of them join your group?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I know that Tavic - I can't recall the first name - he had sort of aid on his leg, an orthopaedic aid, and we took him up. As for the others, I didn't see them join us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. And as you -- as the column moved on, what, if anything, happened, after having encountered these, the wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I heard shooting behind us. I assume that they were dead, that they had been killed, but I didn't see that. I didn't turn back to see, then or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say "they," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Well, the Muslims, the Mujahedin. They were the only ones who were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I was referring to the portion of your answer where you said "they were dead." Who were you referring to when you said "they"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I didn't say that they were dead. I say that only it was only the Muslims who were armed, and I believe that it was the Muslims and the Mujahedin that had opened fire when this column had set off; these wounded people, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you said you heard shooting behind you, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then you said that you assumed that they were dead, that they had been killed. Who are these people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people who were at hospital in Maline. There was this woman, then Luka was also with them. I know about Luka and the woman, and I don't know the names of the other people. And as for Tavic, we took him with us. Whether anyone else joined our column, I didn't see. But as we had advanced some 70 metres or so, I heard shots; and I assumed that the fire had been opened at them, but I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Does that help you, Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, what, if anything happened, when you -- when the group reached Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Well, we took the road. The column took this road up to the village of Bikosi, and the first people came across a house enclosed with a stonewall. It wasn't very high, perhaps one metre. The front man jumped over the wall and started fleeing. The Muslims opened fire at him; and then, later, this one lad, Mijo Tavic, who was an epileptic, I heard him scream and then they opened fire at us, at the column. I then turned around and I threw myself on my belly on the ground. That was when I was -- when I took a hit in my chest and in my leg, and Jako Tavic fell on top of me. I could hear him moaning. I knew that he was wounded, so I just lay there trying to hide. How long I lay there, I don't know. I heard someone get up and flee. Later, I myself also got up and I fled into the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, did you hear anything when you were lying on your stomach?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They were still shooting at us. At first, they shot at us, then the fire stopped, and then there were individual shots. I believe that they were shooting at people who were still giving signs of life, and I tried to hide. I lay low. I didn't move. When I heard that someone had jumped up and ran away, I did so myself, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, where was the -- in relation to where -- in relation to where the soldiers were standing, where was the -- the soldiers that were -- sorry, the Mujahedin and the other soldiers that had been guarding you, where was the wall?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Near the first person who was the first person in the column at the front end, who jumped over the wall as soon as we came to the wall. After jumping over the wall, he then, when they started shooting, ran away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Were the soldiers who were guarding you, were they in front of that wall?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: No. No. They went parallel with us. They were actually -- they were actually guarding us, escorting us, and they had taken such positions as to be able to see all of us. This other person was down there at a right angle in relation to the wall, and he actually went around the house, so that this person who came to the wall actually planned to jump over it and run away once we reached the wall, and that's what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, what happened to the Jako Tavic, the man that was standing next to you in the column? You said he was wounded. Did he survive this incident?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: No. No. He died as he lay on top of me. I believe that he was hit in the head. I could hear his death rattle for a while. And after that, all was still.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pranjes, if you could have another look at the map in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I'd ask that he use the blue pen to make the markings that I'm going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If you could indicate the path that you took from the point where you were separated from the group that was going towards Mehurici, the path that you took from that point until the incident in Bikosi; and, again, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: You cannot see the road leading past Bikosi, but I'll do it approximately, if that's okay. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you mark with a number 2 the point at which the shooting began?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I don't see exactly that road where we were. I cannot mark it with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But to the best of your --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: This is thereabouts. We passed by the -- through the centre of the village, and there was a water trough there, sort of a water reservoir. I can't exactly mark where it was. It's more or less the centre of the village or a bit further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, Mr. Pranjes.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Well, I should put this mark here. [Marks] It was around this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you place -- can you mark it with the number 2?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 133.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, you had indicated that you fled after the shooting. Where did you eventually end up?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I went up towards the Serbian forces, to Babanovac. Later, I was exchanged at Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: How far is -- how far away is Babanovac from Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. Perhaps 60 or 70 kilometres or perhaps less, but I'm not sure. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in which direction is it in relation to Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: It is to the west of Bikosi. One has to go over Vlasic towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to reach Babanovac?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I didn't dare move during the day. I spent the whole day in the nearby woods. Actually, I stayed there just until dawn, then I went through the forest towards Brloge. This was a sort of a pasture for our herds. We had a shed there. Actually, we tended our sheep there, so it is called Brloge. I wanted then to continue on, but then I heard a shot from the direction to which I planned to go, so that I stopped there and stayed there over the night. And I observed the road which was below me throughout the night. There were Muslims on the road, and there were people who kept their sheep and cows and horses on the mountain. They were driving these people in front of them. I lay low in the mountain. I waited for night to fall. When it was dark, I went to outside Suhi Dol because there was water there and I was thirsty, so I had a drink of water. I found something to also eat. Then I went up and across the village of Orlice; and then I went, took a left turn to what is called Ravne, where there is a relay, and then on towards Vlasic where there was the Serb army. There, I surrendered to them, and then they escorted me down to Babanovac. Down there I found this lad, Drago Pranjes. He had also surrendered. He was there in the village, and there was also Stjepan Juric. That was on that day, and then there were also refugees from Travnik up there in Babanovac. They were waiting for trucks to transport them to Croatia. In the afternoon, I don't know exactly when, they all left and I remained on; then sometime around midnight --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pranjes. I think that's fairly clear now how long you took in reaching Babanovac. And as I understand it, you were eventually exchanged at Kiseljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, in the end at Kiseljak. For a while, I was in Manjaca. From Manjaca, we went to Vares with all these civilians from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No further questions, your honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It will then be the proper time to take a break. Court adjourned we will come back at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon, I'm sorry to do this in the middle of your -- you've just finished examining the witness, but I'm sorry to do this in the middle of the witness's testimony. But just this one little housekeeping matter. I guess there has been a suggestion that we sit this afternoon to try and cover up on time. I think, from the Trial Chamber's view point, we can sit from 3.00 and we can go up to about 5.00 or so. Is that okay with everybody?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm being advised by my boss that we can't go up to 5.00. We can only go up to 4.30, so it will be one and a half hours. Thank you very much. You were done, Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pranjes. My name is Nicholas Robson, and I'll be asking you some questions for the Defence. I hope I'll be brief. You told us, just before the break, that you grew up in Maline in Travnik municipality; but in 1990, you moved abroad to Switzerland; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Then, in September 1992, you returned back to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you moved back to your home village of Maline?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And towards the end of that year, you joined the Frankopan Brigade of the Croatian Defence Council, is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you confirm that most of the Bosnian Croat men, from the village of Maline and the other Bosnian Croat villages around, those that were fit for military service joined that brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that when you returned to Bosnia, what you found was that Serb forces had established front lines throughout the Travnik region and especially on Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And your brigade organised or your brigade had organised defensive lines facing the Serbs on that mountain?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just go back to that last answer for a moment, I note that there is no interpretation. My understanding is that the witness confirmed that Serb forces had indeed established front lines throughout the Travnik region, especially on Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you get the witness to answer that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise, witness. Please, again, could you just confirm that, when you returned to Bosnia, you found that the Serbs had established front lines throughout the Travnik region, and you could find them upon Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in addition to the Frankopan Brigade organising defensive lines against the Serbs, it's correct to say that the Bosnian Muslims from Maline village and the other surrounding Muslim villages had also organised defensive lines against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Moving on to events in 1993, you told the Chamber how relations between the HVO and the Bosnian army deteriorated. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You explained to the Chamber how in your village the HVO set up guards, and you explained to us the defensive lines from Maline up along Greda to Suhi Dol, is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And those defensive lines were manned by soldiers from the Croatian Defence Council, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: It was just us from the village there. There were about ten men of us local men from the village of Maline. We held those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us about the events that occurred on the 8th of June 1993, but I'd just like to ask you a question about the days leading up to that particular date. It's right, isn't it, that the Croatian Defence Council carried out attacks on a number of Bosnian Muslim villages in those days before the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, as to the attack on Maline that you told us about, am I right in understanding that, on the evening of 7th of June, you were on guard duty with three others?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, I was, in the evening of the 6th and of the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is it right that were you wearing a uniform at that time, a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the three other men, they were all wearing military uniforms as well?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You explained that the attack started about 5.00 on the morning of the 8th of June. It's right, isn't it, that there was heavy fighting, and the fighting went on for a considerable period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Where? Where do you mean? In Maline or at some other place?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: At Maline, on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: The attack had been mounted on the 8th of June at 5.00 in the morning. It started by two stables being set on fire in Bikosi, and I assume that that was a signal for a frontal attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree that there was heavy fighting that took place that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And at some point in time, you decided to withdraw from your position and go to your relative's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that some of the HVO soldiers were able to escape from Maline and make their way towards Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You explained that the home of your relative had been turned into a makeshift hospital, and you told us how the doctor at that place went out to speak to the members of the Bosnian army. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that after terms of surrender were discussed, you handed over your weapon to the Bosnian army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I hid my weapon in the basement, near the hospital under a slab. It wasn't really finished. There was a bin with corn there, in fact, and that's where I actually hid a pistol and a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, at some point in time, you explained how a soldier, who appeared to be in charge, told the Bosnian Croats to gather together in the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were 300 people that gathered together. Did this -- was this a collection of civilians and HVO soldiers that had surrendered?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, then, at some point in time, you all moved in one column, ought of the village, in the direction of Mehurici, is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that the Bosnian army soldiers treated you professionally whilst they were gathering you together and whilst the column was moving along out of the village?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And that column that you told us about made its way through Poljanice village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And once the column had passed through Poljanice, you explained to us that a number of Mujahedin jumped out. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
