utterances.text: As I understood your evidence, there were four or five Mujahedin that were close to you, and there were a number of other Mujahedin, about 15 metres away from you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I said wearing masks. I said that there were those wearing masks or hats on their faces, and the others were Mujahedin. They were both very close to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The Mujahedin, they were the men that had dark skin and long beards; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, these men, the Mujahedin and the others wearing masks, they stopped the column, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you remember whereabouts you were in the column?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: In the back part of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, those men you told us about, the Mujahedin and the men wearing masks, they were carrying guns with them, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: They pointed the guns at you and the Bosnian soldiers that were accompanying your column, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right that they cocked their weapons so that they were ready to fire; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The Bosnian army soldiers that were escorting you tried to stop the Mujahedin from taking the men from that column, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: A little earlier in your evidence, you said something like the one I thought was the commander shouted, "Command, command." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that what you meant by that was that the leader or the commander of the Bosnian Muslim soldiers that were escorting you was trying to point out to the Mujahedin that they were taking you to their command centre?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it was only when the Mujahedin pointed their guns at threatened to shoot the Bosnian army members that the Mujahedin were able to separate the Bosnian Croat men from the column; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the Bosnian army soldiers couldn't do anything to prevent that, could they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, then, the Bosnian Croat men were separated from the column, and the new group of Bosnian Croat men were moved in the direction of Mehurici by the Mujahedin, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: The Mujahedin and those people wearing masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And from that point, you and the other Bosnian Croat men, accompanied by the Mujahedin and the men wearing masks, continued on your way in the direction of Bikosi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, I have no further questions for you. I certainly don't wish to ask you about the incident that occurred in Bikosi, again, so thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. Could I just say something, Mr. Robson? I chose to not to say it an at the proper time when it was happening. I'm just mentioning it now, because it does happen quite often. And let me prefix what I'm going to say by declaring up front that I do accept that, in cross-examining a witness, it is necessary, at times, to refresh his memory and focus his point on a particular incident that you want to talk about. But I just find that you ask a series of questions that are repetitive of evidence-in-chief, which are not necessarily linked to the point you want to get to eventually, and that consumes a bit of time. I just want to -- I'm just throwing it as a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I take that as a constructive comment, and I'm grateful for you stating that. Obviously, as you say, some of the questions were aimed with a view to making some specific points to the witness, and I have tried to reduce my number of questions to a minimum as well. But I, certainly, take on board your comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you look at the questions that you asked at the beginning of your cross-examination, you'll find that there was quite a series of them, and I just didn't see the link to the point you were going to make finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Any re-examination, Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, you had indicated in cross-examination that, prior to the 8th of June, that there had been attacks by the Croatian Defence Council against Bosnian Muslim villages. Could you indicate which villages you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Only in Bukovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Menon. Any further questions, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have a couple of questions in relation to what you have explained in examination-in-chief and cross-examination. The first question is related to your surrender to the Serbs on the 9th of June or the 10th of June, a couple of days after the incident?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were you taken prisoner by the Serbs when you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And were you detained?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Up to midnight, I was in Babanovac, at the hotel there; and after that, they took me to Vitovlje, where the main command was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And for how long did you sit there.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: On the following day, we were taken to Manjaca, and that's where I stayed with all the other civilians from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: For how long before you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I spent one or two nights at Manjaca, and then we were taken to Vares in lorries. We spent some ten to 15 days in Vares. From Vares we were taken to Kiseljak and exchanged. It took us a day to get from Vares to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So that if I understand you correctly, you were detained by the Serbs altogether for a supple of weeks, three weeks perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Approximately, two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My second question relates to the incident in Poljanice, because it is a bit unclear to me, and I realise this is a long time ago and it's probably unclear to you what really happened. But I am not sure I fully understand the interactions between the men who jumped out in front of you, as you were marching towards Mehurici. What I have understood is that you came marching in a column, and you were escorted by some members of the ABiH. And from all that I have understood, these ABiH soldiers were behaving professionally and correctly. They were just marching you up towards Mehurici, but then comes the incident where suddenly some other soldiers were jumping out in front of you. Some of them, we understand, were clearly different from what you had seen before. They were wearing beards and had strange uniforms, and they were talking a foreign language. Together with these - I don't know how many there were, but three or four - Mujahedins, were also a small number of what you think were Bosnian soldiers and members of the ABiH. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see the Defence counsel rising on his feet, and I would like to hear the Defence's intervention because I think it's important to figure out exactly what the composition was here. So that's why I'm putting my finger in it. Mr. Robson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would suggest that the witness be removed from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: For what purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, any questions that might be put to Your Honour by Defence counsel might prejudice the witness's view of the events, I would be afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm really trying to elicit an almost full picture of what happened, and I think it would be useful to hear the Defence counsel's questions and for you, if you wish to put further questions, that may arise out of this line of questioning. I think you should be entitled to. But I don't think it would be incorrect to allow the witness to hear the questions from the Defence counsel, but please let me hear your arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: My position was as I had stated it. I think the witness has answered the question that Your Honour put to him. If Defence counsel were to, in their question, if their comments to Your Honour, if they were to suggest some other impression, then I would be afraid that the witness's -- the witness's view of the events might be prejudiced, and that might affect any other further answers that he might give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But the witness has obviously just answered my question in such a manner that in a manner that contradicts the answer that he gave previously to the Defence counsel. So there is a clearly a contradiction between the witness's answers to the two questions; one put by me and one put by the Defence counsel. Now, I believe that this contradiction is probably because the witness's memory may be defused. As I said, it's a long time ago. If the witness cannot remember, I will urge the witness to tell me so, and that's the end of the story. If, however, he has another understanding, then I think we should allow him to express it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And if that gives you rise to questions, you should, of course, be entitled to put them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So thank you. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I would support my friend's application, if you were to think -- if you were to wish to ask this witness further questions. I rise -- well, I rose initially to initially to essentially make a point pertaining to the record, the transcript. And I wished to draw Your Honour's attention to what had been recorded during the course of this witness's testimony. Obviously, Your Honour, I can make this point in the presence of the witness, but I would suggest -- I would concur with my friend, the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, you made a statement that if Your Honour were to put your question to the witness, you would concur with your colleague that the witness must go out. Now, there is some kind of problem that I have with that. How is the question put to the witness if the witness is out?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry. The point that I was trying to make is that if the either Judge Harhoff or another one of your other colleagues wished to put a further question to this witness, then it would be appropriate, in my belief, to perhaps have this discussion for me to make the points that I wish to make in the absence of the witness. That way, the witness would not be privy to that discussion and, therefore, Your Honours would be able to put further questions to him, without fear that perhaps he may have been influenced as a result of the discussions that I need to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem is that I'm not privy to what it is you want to talk about, and, therefore, I'm not able to make a determination whether the witness must get out or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll go ahead and raise the point. The issue, as I say, pertains to the record of what this witness said during his testimony; and with respect to Judge Harhoff, the question that he asked was -- sorry. I've written it down according to my note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me assist you. I was asking about the interplay, the interaction between the members who jumped out in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And I was saying, as I had understood, there were four, let's call them now, Mujahedin and four or five Bosnians with masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Correct. And it was at that point, Your Honour -- so you referred to the foreigners, let's put it that way, and then you said -- referred to what you think were Bosnian soldiers and members of the ABiH. That was the -- those were the words you used and put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Correct me, is that controversial?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a matter of record, at no stage did this witness ever use the words "Bosnian soldiers," and at no other stage did he suggest that those men with the Mujahedin wearing the masks were members of the ABiH. That was the position during the directs examination and cross-examination. So it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You may be correct. I'm sorry. I would then proceed with asking the witness if he could tell us if he recognised any uniform or insignia on the members of the gentlemen with masks. Would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Prosecution, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Witness, I'm sorry if this has been confusing to you, but you understand that there is a problem relating to the identification of the gentlemen who were wearing masks. And my question to you, therefore, is: Were these men wearing uniforms? If you cannot remember, then just tell me so.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They wore green uniforms. They did wear uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We are now talking about the men with masks.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes. They wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia or marks on the arms on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember that they had them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you hear them speak, and could you understand what they were saying?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I could not understand those who did not wear masks, but I did understand those who did wear masks on their faces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So am I right to assume that you did not know for sure which army they may have belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They belonged to the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And how can you say this?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: May I say something, or rather, may I ask you something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I know that the Mujahedin had their camp where they lived. They had arrived there while I was still in Switzerland. And I know that they trained Muslim soldiers, that they trained them, that they also learned -- taught them how to speak differently. I know that during the attack, not a single word was used in the Muslim or in the Croato-Serbian or Serbo-Croat for attack, only "Tekbir" and "Allah U Ekber." Those were the only words that we could hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: So I leave it up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. But could the men with masks not just as well have been Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: No chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Where would the Serb soldiers have come from to arrive in Mehurici? How would they have found themselves there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave this question of who they were, and I'm satisfied with your answer. And I understand that you thought they were Bosnians, but you could not tell for sure. I would like then to move on to what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because you also testified that the Mujahedin at some point raised their guns and threatened the soldiers with masks.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Not those wearing masks but the others, the Bosnian soldiers, who were going to take us to Mehurici. They threatened them. They shouted at them. They said to them that they would separate us. The commander who was there, he was shouting, "Command, command." But as I heard that, a lot more Mujahedin had been down there. I suppose that they prevailed, that they had a majority, these Mujahedin, and the others had to give in. That's why we had to be given to them, to them to do with us whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what happened to the soldiers who had escorted you from Maline up towards Mehurici? Did they continue with the rest of the column?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They left with the others towards Mehurici. They escorted the other civilians; the children, the women, and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you were then escorted back towards Bikosi where you had just come from?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: When the incident occurred - and I'm sorry, again, that I will just ask you one question in relation to this terrible incident - did you see if it was only the Mujahedin who were shooting or were the men with masks also shooting?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They were all shooting, both the men in masks and the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Nothing further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, you always come first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. No questions from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not even after I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't even know what I'm going to ask. Mr. Pranjes, when you talk about "Mujahedin," what do you mean by that term?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Well, these were foreign soldiers who came to wage war, side by side with the Muslim army. These are foreigners who came to Bosnia to fight a war. They had long beards, and they could not speak Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So by "Mujahedin," in your understanding, you imagine foreigners and foreigners only?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They were foreigners until they arrived there. Once they had arrived, they no longer were foreigners; they took Muslim wives. They would have two or three of them. Some would go to -- to their homes, and they would stay together with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, but all I'm trying to get from you is that your understanding of the concept "Mujahedin" is that this is a group of people composed of people who originally came from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that you don't include in there any locals?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You talked about, when you were asked questions by Judge Harhoff, of being detained for approximately two weeks. Can you tell us how you were treated during that time in detention?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: They treated us fairly up there. We had no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you also talked about some soldiers wearing green uniforms, do you remember that; again, during questions by Judge Harhoff?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know to which army those uniforms belonged?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes, I know. They belonged to the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "the Muslim army"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: The army of the BH; to me, that is the same thing. I refer to it as the ABiH army or that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. At least now we know what you mean by "Muslim army." And you also talked about - and I'm sorry, again, to bring you back to this terrible incident - the shooting that took place at Bikosi; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us how many people were killed, if any at all, on that occasion? You may not have counted, just an approximation.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but over 30 people were killed there. Three or four of us managed to escape. The rest were killed. Some of them were killed down there on the road as they were speaking to flee; and Jako, for instance, died atop of me. Ana Pranjes, a relative, was also killed there; and, later, a mass grave was also found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry. I didn't mean to bring those memories, but I guess you understand it is important for us to get answers to some of these questions. Thank you very much. That concludes my questions. Any questions arising from the questions from the Bench, Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour. Further Re-examination by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, you had indicated that you were detained for two weeks. Who was responsible for your detention? Who was --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: It was the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And were these the forces that you had -- that you had turned yourself into, after fleeing the incident at Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: Yes. I surrendered to the Serbian army up there at Vlasic, and then they took me to Manjaca --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the witness's sentence. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Pranjes, the interpreter didn't hear the full sentence that you just recited, if you could repeat that.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO PRANJES
utterances.text: The Serbian army, I surrendered to the Serbian army at Vlasic, and then they took me to -- through Vlasic up to Manjaca, and then to Vares. And the Croats were still in Vares; then they put us aboard buses and we went to Kiseljak, where I stayed until the end of the war and where I was eventually exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pranjes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Menon. Mr. Robson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Pranjes, this brings us to the end of your testimony, and let me take the opportunity just to thank you very much for coming to testify. You are now excused. You may stand down. And, once again, just I'm sorry for causing you that. Judge Harhoff has something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would like to add something, Mr. Pranjes, if you would. This is perhaps unusual, but I would like to take this opportunity to also express the compassion and sympathy from the Bench for the suffering that you have had, and we hope that your testimony today does not disturb your state of mind too much. We wish you good travel back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, the Prosecution calls Zeljko Puselja, and my colleague Mr. Wood will be leading this witness, and I would also just indicate for the report that we have been joined by our intern, Allessandro Bernosconi, who will be assisting us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, it will proceed until the regular 1.45?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may be seated and good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Mr. Puselja.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court your name, spelling your first and last name for the record?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: It is Z-E-L-J-K-O, P-U-S-E-L-J-A.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Where were you born, Mr. Puselja?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I was born in Travnik, in B and H.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, when you say "Travnik," do you mean Travnik municipality or a specific village within that municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: The municipality of Travnik, and the village of Podovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: The 9th of March 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What is your nationality or ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were you living in Podovi in 1993, Mr. Puselja?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At that time, were you a member of any military organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of a military organisation, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: In 1993, I was a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when did you join the HVO, if you could tell the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but with the dismantling of the TO, the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Puselja, what was the ethnic composition of the village in which you resided in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: It was a Croat village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were there other villages in your area where the ethnic composition was different from that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what were some of those other villages?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Pode, a Muslim village; Han Bila, also a Muslim village; Fazlici, a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I want to ask you some questions about the first half of 1993. Were there any Serbs in your area at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And where were they living?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Though were living in the village of Savici near Poljanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And did they remain there throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall, if you know, when they left?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What makes you say that you know they didn't remain there throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Because after 1993, after the 8th of June, there were Arabs in their village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how far is this village from Poljanice or Mehurici, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I can't say with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Would it be more than 500 metres?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: No, not from Poljanice. From Mehurici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, this village was called Savici. What was the last name of the people who lived there, the majority of them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I couldn't say, because I never was up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In the first half of 1993, could you please describe the relations between the Croat community and the Muslim community in your area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Relations used to be normal and excellent. We went to school together in Mehurici, which is their chief village, where we had our shops, we had the shopping malls, stores, and infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did there come a time when this changed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, it all changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, before the 8th of June, Mr. Puselja, had you ever seen any foreigners in your area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And could you describe when, under what circumstances, you saw them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I saw them in Mehurici, by the school. I can't say on what exact date I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were there any other occasions when you saw foreigners in your area, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes. We -- I did see them because we had a football field which was called the Lager, and I used to see them very often before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how far is that area from your village, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Between three and four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how did you know that these people were foreigners, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Well, when I saw them, I could tell, because the locals usually did not wear beards and stuff, and these people did wear beards -- did have beards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What were these foreigners doing when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Those that I saw at Mehurici with this emir, before the conflict, they were bound for Vlasic, up there; at least that is what I heard from neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And the foreigners you saw at Lager, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: There were two of them there. We were playing soccer, and they were standing on the left side of the road. One of them was holding a map and explaining something to this other guy. He was pointing to our village and showing something to him with his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were the foreigners alone, or were they with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: There were just the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how far were you from these foreigners when you saw them there at Lager?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Between 30 and 50 metres, not more than that. That is how far the main road was from the pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned 8 June 1993, sir. I'm going to ask you some questions about that now. Do you recall where you were in the morning of 8 June 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I was at the entrance to the village of Podstinje Donje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And you mentioned that your home village is Podovi. Could you explain to the Court why you were in Podstinje that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, late in the afternoon, we all retreated up to Podstinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want it clarify something for the record. You said, "On the 8th of June, we all retreated up to Podstinje," but my question to you was: Early in the morning on the 8th of June, why is it that you were in Podstinje rather than in Podovi, which you indicated earlier was your home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you understand the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'll move on. It's okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I would like to get an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why did you retreat to Podstinje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had to retreat because when Miletici suffered in April or May, we were told that we would not be able to defend our village, and this was the only corridor that we would go to from Podstinje to Maline. If we stayed, we would have been completely encircled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is meant by the "Miletici"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is also a Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you said you alone retreated. You say, "I had to retreat." Was it only you who retreated, or were you with other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We all had to retreat, the civilians and however many soldiers were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the 8th of June, everything changed. What was your first indication on the 8th of June that things were changing in your area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: First of all, there were provocations from Fazlici. Around 7.00 or 8.00, they opened fire on our village, but we did not react to those provocations in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when you say they opened fire from Fazlici, was that before the 8th of June or on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Even before that day, a few days before, they started opening fire on us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who are the "they" who opened fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, again, sir, I want to ask you specifically about 8 June 1993. At what time did you wake up on that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Was there an attack on the 8th of June 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when did that attack begin?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Around 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How did you know that the attack was beginning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: As I've already told you, I was in Podstinje at the entrance of the village keeping guard down there, and then the artillery cannon fire started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you determine, sir, from which direction the artillery was coming?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: From the direction of Poljanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What happened after the mortars started falling, sir? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: We were there for some 15 or 20 minutes, providing security to the village of Podstinje, and then Goran Bobic joined us. He said that they managed to repel the first brunt of that attack, but that the lines were falling up there and that we should start retreating to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you in fact retreat, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the village of Podstinje?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: As we approached the village of Gornji Podstinje [as interpreted], we proceeded straight on in the direction of Maline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were the mortars still falling at this time, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Why is it that you close to retreat toward the direction of Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: That was the only way out. There was no where else to go. This was the only place where we could retreat to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what made you believe that Gornje Maline was a safe place to retreat to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: There was no where else to go. Maline was the only corridor for us to go through if we wanted to go anywhere, if we wanted to go on. Everything around us was blocked. There was no where else to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of Gornje Maline, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: There were two villages: Donje and Gornje Maline. I personally am familiar with entire Maline; Donji were Muslim and Gornje were Croat population. So there were two ethnically pure villages, Gornje and Donje Maline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what was the nationality of those who lived in Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you. What route did you take to go from Podstinje to Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: We went through a little forest and then through a meadow called Vranjaca, across the sand pit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers at this time, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: When we arrived at that sand pit, we did not see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At what time did you see the forces that were -- what time, if any, did you see the forces that were attacking you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, coming from the forest and from the meadow, I could see some soldiers approaching. That's when we were in that sand pit or patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you determine, sir, what army these soldiers were from?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I couldn't see them properly, but I saw that they were wearing uniforms; and then when every village around us fell up there, I could see them properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And, at that time, could you determine what army they were from, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: The BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you got to that sandy area. How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Not very long. Everything happened very quickly. They started coming from the right-hand side. We had to move quickly; and then ahead of us on the road to Bikosi, I saw Tomo falling down. He had been hit. I realised that that was very close, and I had to head quickly towards the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When you say "they" were coming from the right-hand side, do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: The Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What do you mean, sir, by "Muslim army"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: The BiH army. It was a predominantly Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony, you just said, "I had to head quickly towards the village," which village was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Gornje Maline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you reach Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I reached as far as the first three houses on the right-hand side, in the place where a cross is standing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Is that cross in Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The cross is in the village of Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes, on a rock on the right side of Maline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Where did you go next, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: We entered a little forest right below the rock. There were four of us, and we were waiting to be able to run across the meadow in order to enter the houses where everybody else was, the civilians, but we never made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What happened, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Well, we were standing there, everything was falling, there were troops in front of us, and we had to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Who were you with when you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: My father, Mijo; myself; Nikica Balta; Antara Balta; Mato Turic; and another person, the sixth person, whose name I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What time was this, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Around 10.00 or between 10.00 and 11.00 maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood how much longer are you likely to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm moving as quickly as I can, Your Honour. I am mindful of the time. I see now why you're asking. I see that we probably will have to come back at 3.00, and I will be as fast as I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. I'm asking in terms of the break. Is this an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It is an appropriate time, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take an adjournment and come back at 3.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Puselja, when we took a break, you had mentioned that you surrendered at about 11.00 a.m. in the village of Gornje Maline. Can you please explain what were the conditions that day? Was it a sunny day or a cloudy day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: It was rather sunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, at the time that you surrendered, were you able to see the forces that had been attacking you in the village of Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you see any foreigners among those troops?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I rose to my feet to object to that leading question. We, obviously, received the answer, but I just would like to put that complaint on record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When you surrendered, what did you do with the weapons you had?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I gave it to the soldier to whom we surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And could you determine what army the soldier was from?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What happened immediately after you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: When we surrendered, they took us across that meadow to the village, and we were there together with the other captured civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How many captured civilians were there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Three hundred, 350.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you had surrendered with a group of five or six of your fellow soldiers. Can you tell the Court, after the group had gathered with the 350 civilians, were there other HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you estimate how many there were, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Fifty-ish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you recognise the soldiers, personally recognise the soldiers, to whom you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how many soldiers, if you could estimate, did you see in Gornje Maline after you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I could not determine the number. I cannot tell how many there were when we surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: After you surrendered, sir, did you see any soldiers from the other side who had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you describe them, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: They lined us up together with the others on the road at Gornje Maline, and they told us to bend our heads and not to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And did they say why you shouldn't look at these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: They said that if we look up, they would kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And did they say why these particular soldiers you shouldn't look at?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: They said something about "Ara Pranje [phoen]," and that's why we decided that they must be Arabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were you able to see these soldiers that they were talking about, the other soldiers said you shouldn't look at?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I saw two picking up the third from the ground around the corner of the house, and they dragged him around the corner of the house so I couldn't see him any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did these two soldiers look like, these two that were carrying the third wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I could see that both of them certainly had beards; and the third one lying on the ground looking from the top, I could see that he had black hair, curly, and he was not very tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you see what was their complexion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: The two, that bent down to pick him up, were dark-skinned, as far as I could see, at least compared to the local people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how far were you from these soldiers when you saw them, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Not even ten metres. They were just in front of us as we were lined up, not more than ten metres, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what were these men wearing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: They had military uniforms on, but a rather brighter green than the usual military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were these men armed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did it appear to you as though they were able to move around freely, around the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just caution you, when counsel for the Defence stands up, before you answer a question, just stop, don't answer the question. Okay. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that last question. I believe it's a leading question. From the evidence that we've heard so far from the witness, we had heard that, initially, he was told to look down. As I understood his evidence, he was looking down. He happened -- he was able to see these two men, but I certainly don't understand or it's not clear to me from the evidence how it could be established that this witness was able to see these two men moving around freely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, is that an objectionable issue or is that something that you can deal with in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- it's just a -- I'd be grateful if my friend who prosecutes could perhaps phrase his questions carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My point precisely. Is there anything objectionable in the manner in which he put the question? If the witness said he was facing down and he's asked if he saw people and he said he saw people, is that is there anything that is objectionable there or is it something that you deal with in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a question that, I would submit, was phrased in such a way that invited the witness to agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, then you must shift the basis of your objection from what you were saying to something else. If you object to the formulation of the question, let that be so; but once you tally it with his ability to see when he was looking down, it looks to me like you were saying he's asking him to contradict himself and he's not allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the complaint was that he was inviting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the objection, sir. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, the objection becomes upheld. Thank you very much. You may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: On that point, Mr. Puselja, if your head was down, how were you able to see this? How were you able to see what the men looked like?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: They did told us to look at the ground, but we were on a slope. So they were below us, down the slope, by the house, and, of course, I looked down and I saw that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And for how long were you able to observe these men?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: A couple of minutes, not long, because they had just picked him up and dragged him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you mentioned that you had been gathered together with a number of civilians and a number of other HVO soldiers. What happened after that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: When we were gathered into a group, then we all set off towards Mehurici. I heard they were taking us to Mehurici, to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how did you proceed toward Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: They took us as a column down towards Maline, then we turned towards Bikosi, and then we took a byroad towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when you say "they," sir, do you know who it was who was escorting you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how do you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I know them by the uniforms and everything else. I know who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did those uniforms look like? What was about those uniforms that was distinctively BiH army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: They were camouflage uniforms with insignia on the sleeves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did this insignia look like, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: On the right sleeve, they had this insignia that looked like - what did I just say? - the lily.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did the men who were escorting you ever speak to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: When they took us through to "pjescara," Semro Krajisnik addressed us and he told us, "You are now captives. We are going to escort you to Mehurici camp."

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Sands. Pjescara is not a place name; It's the sands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I understand from the interpreter what she means by "sands"? What is sands?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A sandy patch. Sands, S-A-N-D-S, sands. They took them through to the sands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you then proceed toward Mehurici like the -- like the person who you indicated spoke said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes. We did move towards Mehurici, up to Bikosi and Poljanice down there, where they started separating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Before we go much further, Mr. Puselja, do you want to correct something in the record? Earlier, you said "when they took us," I believe, "pjescara," that was corrected, the interpretation doesn't indicate who it was who addressed you and told you, "You are now captives. We are going to escort you to the Mehurici camp." Can you please tell the Court who was that person who said that to you and to the other POW?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Semro, S-E-M-R-O, Krajisnik. We called him Krajisnik because he hailed from Krajina. And when they took us from the sands to the left, towards Bikosi, he came walking towards us. He told us to take off all our religious items, such as crosses on chains and all the HVO insignia we had on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And did he explain why it is that you should do this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: He said we would be walking by the Arabs and to take all that off.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Getting back to what you said earlier, you mentioned a point at which they separated us after you had proceeded toward Mehurici. Who was it that you refer to when you say "they," sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: When we got down to Poljanice and Bikosi, up to that moment, they took us walking on a road; and, at that point, from the left-hand side of the road, Arabs came running at us. They wanted to pick whom they wanted from the column. Semro told them they were captives of the BH army, and the other man said, "Oh, screw the BH army." And then they started an argument, wherein this Arab man put a gun barrel into Semro's mouth. And when that happened, Semro had to give in to the man who wanted to take his pick from the column, that they started doing that, picking men from our group as they pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see at page 88, line 12 -- I'm sorry, line 11 you say, "Arabs came running at us." Can you tell the Court how many there were?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, at that moment, four of them came running from the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And was that the entire group that came running from the side?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: No. Later on, some more came; one was an Arab and four had black masks on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I just want to clarify, sir, how did you know the ones you were referring to as Arabs, how did you know that they were Arabs?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Because the local ones wore masks on their heads. The Arabs didn't. And all our lives we had never seen such men in our area. All of them had beards, and the one that shot at me was a very large man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How did you know, Mr. Puselja, that the ones who wore masks were local, were not Arabs?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Well, because they probably put masks on in order not to be recognised because people must have known them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you hear them speak?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: You mean the Arabs?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Any member of this group that you said came running on to the road.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: The Arab that put a gun into Semro's mouth kept arguing in a language I didn't understand at all, and I only understood when the other answered that we were captives of the BH army, and then the Arab answered in a very accented Bosnian, "Screw the BH army."

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So what did the man you referred to as Semro, what did he do after the gun was put into his mouth?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Well, he had to give in, I suppose, since the others started taking their pick of the men. He just motioned with his arm that he was giving in, so that the other one would take the barrel out of his mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how many -- how many men or how many people were separated out of the group?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Well, I concluded that four or five of us were singled out. There were nine of them, and they made a group of five prisoners; and when the one who was speaking came up to me, he pointed the barrel of the gun into my stomach and he said, "You, too; you, too."

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If you could please tell the Court what were you wearing when this happened, Mr. Puselja?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I had military pants and a brown jumper on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If you recall, sir, who were some of the other members of the group who were separated out by these Arabs?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Some also had military uniforms or bits of uniforms, but there were also civilians, including children of 13 or 14 and elderly men -- elderly people. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: After this group had been separated out, where did the remainder of the group go?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: They took them to Mehurici, to the camp in the school house; I mean, the group of civilians that stayed down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And in which direction did the other group go, the smaller group that had been separated out?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Well, those of us who were singled out, they took us back, but not using the same road. They took us along a narrow path through the woods where only carts could pass, and they took us back to Bikosi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the people who were in this smaller group, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes. Vlado Puselja was one; Niko Bobas, Goran Bobas, father and son; Dalibor and Stipo Jankovic, father and son; Barac, Pavo and Bojan, brothers; then Pero Bobas; Sreco Bobas, also; Ana Pranjes; Ivo Tavic; Buco of father Niko Jurcevic; and then Franjo Puselja, father Vinko; Anto, Jozo, and Nikica Balta, the three Balta brothers. These were the people whom I knew from my village. And there was also Tavic, Ivo, and these people that I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: One name that you mentioned, Ana Pranjes. Can you tell the Court what was she wearing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: She had a top motley coloured jacket, but she had a Red Cross patch. She was the assistant of Dr. Ljubica, and she had a white jersey or a white T-shirt also on her.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, this Ana Pranjes, where were you in relation to her in the group?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. Let me ask again --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Oh, she was in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did anything happen to Ana Pranjes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes. This short, very thin Arab, perhaps only 60 kilograms of weight, with black, curly hair, he walked up to her and he touched her on the stomach, asked her if she was pregnant, if she was married, and such things. She was wearing a chain with a pendant with "Our Lady" on the pendant, and he ripped it off her neck and threw it away. She wanted to lit a cigarette. He ripped the cigarette out of her mouth and threw that away, too. Then the second Arab walked up and said, "Go, Go," meaning to fetch her some cigarettes, and then he continued asking her about her. He actually touched her on the jacket and asked her to take it off, asking her why did she need to wear it. She was very courageous, I believe, so she just buttoned up her jacket, and she said, "If I'm to die, I'm going to do so in the uniform of my country." And then he grabbed her bay the waist, and then he sort of pushed her to the left side, and then he fired a burst into her.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: They took us farther up to Bikosi by the same small path. They lined us up in front of the first house to the left, so that was the house of Ljuba of Matija; Ljuba being the wife of the husband Matija, that's how we say it. So when we were lined up on the left side, this small, slender, blond guy who had this cap with slots for the eyes started interrogating us to the effect, Who was a sniper, Who was this or that. And this Arab who had shot me personally, he came and he actually tapped him on the shoulder, and that's when I remember his name, he said, "Isak, you are Allah." And this other one went into Ljuba's house, this first house on the left side. He went into the house. We heard him shout, "Allah U Ekber," then he came out of the house and was pointing his finger showing to this other guy something. And this other guy sort of motioned with his head to ask him what he was indicating, and he just pointed his finger, this guy who had come out of the house, towards down. This other one went behind the house. I thought that there was a well there, but it turned out that there was a chicken coop there, in fact. So he had us go back to the road, and he made this gesture with his hand, showing that he should kill us and throw us into the well. That's, in fact, why I first thought that it was a well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like the report to reflect that when the witness said -- he made a gesture, he took his hand and dragged it across his neck. Just so that's clear in the written record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned this person named "Isak." Was he one of the people who had been wearing a mask previously?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. One of them. And then after they had lined us up there in front of this house, on the right side, we were standing there. The others took off their masks, and I recognised one; a big, brawny, dark man. He used to work with my father; and, later, I told my father how he looked, but my father could not remember his name. And I also recognised this other one who was big and blond. He had a store at the entrance to Mehurici on the right side. He is perhaps a head taller than I myself, and he is quite bigger than I am. And this fourth man who was there, he was dark-haired and slender, and he's Zihnad Sejdic. That is the name I heard later in camp. That is his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: This Zihnad Sejdic, did you come to learn the name of his father?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Later, in the camp, after all this was over, we discussed things among ourselves again in Mehurici, and I described to some people how he looked. And Zarko Balta, who lived near them, near the village of Sejdici, said, on the basis of my description, that there was the possibility that that could be these people, the Sejdicis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again, sir. Did you come to know what this person's -- what his father's name was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: We can come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. What have you forgotten, sir? Have you forgotten the father's name, or have you forgotten whether he came to know his fathers's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had told me in the camp his father's name, but I have another gotten his father's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the answer to the question is you did come to know the father's name, but you just can't remember it now? That's the answer you want to give?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Puselja, do you remember giving a statement to the ICTY about this incident?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And do you remember, in that statement, providing the name of the father of this person?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I believe that I did, but at this point I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And that statement was given in September of 2006; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Would it refresh your recollection, or would it assist you in refreshing your recollection, if you were able to see that statement again?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I believe that it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could have the usher please show a copy of this statement to the witness, and if that could be placed on to the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. This is his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the witness please identify the statement, the document, before he's asked about the contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Puselja, if you could take a look at that document, is that document a copy of the statement that you provided to the ICTY in 2006? And if I could ask you please take it off the ELMO and take a good look at it, to make sure that that is your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes. This is definitely my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is your signature on it, sir? Did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might intervene, I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: His signature does in the appear on this. This is a translation of the statement that he provided to the ICTY. How it works is: He provides the statement, it's simultaneously transcribed in to English, then read back to the witness. The English version is what he signs. For the purposes of making things easier, this is a copy of his statement translated into B/C/S. So his statement -- his signature does not appear on this document; although, this is a translation of a signed statement that the witness provided in 2006, as reflected on the front page of the statement that is in front of him right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wood. You can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Puselja, having taken a look at that statement, is your memory refreshed about the name of the father of the person that you were speaking of, this Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is Zihnad Sejdic, who is the son of Zahid Sejdic and they are from the Sejdici village. Zahid is the name of the father of Zihnad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: This person named "Isak," did you come to find out his last name?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I, again, found that out in the camp. I described him to Zarko Balta, and they told me that there was just this one Isak, the son of Isak Aganovic from the village of Fazlici. I described his looks to the people in the camp. He looked like Zarko Balta quite a lot, but he was a bit thinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, sir, just to clarify then, you came to though that this person's name was Isak Aganovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: When we were being executed up there, when the Arab told him, "Isak, you are Allah," I remembered his name and his face. And then in the camp, I described the different people and their looks to the people in the camp, and I told them his name. And they then told me that this could be this man, Isak Aganovic, the son of Rasid from Fazlici; whereas, I personally did not know that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned another person, a person who had a shop. Do you recall the name of this person?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: He had a shop on the right side, after the entry point to the -- to Mehurici, on a small hillock. His name was Vehbija Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I think that's all we'll need with the statement for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Puselja, you mentioned, before I was asking you these questions about the names, that they had lined you up. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: After they had lined us up in groups, at the moment, when I said that there was a well outside by the asphalt road, Mijo Tavic, who was with us, was an epileptic. And as we were standing up there, I was in the second or third group, he had a fit and he started screaming and started crying out. They became scared and they opened fire. This one who was standing in front of me, some metre or metre and a half away from me, I saw him. I saw him start to take to the ground, and I myself turned and took to the ground. And as I was falling, a bullet hit me in my right elbow. As I was falling, my arm gave in the shoulder and I hit my face on the asphalt, and then I lay on the road pretending to be dead. Ican Volic fell on my feet. From the left side, I could see that his guts had been torn and I could hear his death rattle. And another person who had been mowed down by the burst also fell on top of me. And that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned there was one person standing in front of you who fired. What did the other people in the group do, the other people in the group of Arabs and others who had escorted you to Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: When we heard the shooting, the burst, you could only hear the moaning and the crying out, and people went every possible way. When we all fell down, one could hear individual shots, and there was one person speaking in our language. One of the locals, who was speaking in our own language, he said, "You take me and then you go on. You continue after that." They were killing off one by one, so that we could only hear individual shots at that point. And as my head was down on the asphalt, I could just see at the sneakers on somebody's feet. I was covered in a lot of blood from me and from other people. So they thought that I was dead so that I could just hear the click of someone stopping a rifle, and then they went on. I continued to furtively listen and look, and I saw two Arabs going up in order to prevent anyone from coming to the site, and they took away this man who was moaning because they could no longer bear to hear his cries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: This man you indicate who was moaning, was he one of the Arab foreigners or was he one of the locals who had been wearing a mask?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: He was definitely one of the locals because he was shouting clear, fluent -- in our language, and I could understand exactly what he was saying. He was saying, "Take me away first, and then go on with your business."

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I realise this is a difficult experience for you, Mr. Puselja, but I need to ask you: Did all of the people in the group fire during the massacre?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: I believe that they did, because when I got up from the -- after the execution, it was -- when I got up, I listened and I saw that there was no one, and then I said, "Oh, my God, I'm alive."

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, you're here today with us, so, obviously, you survived this. Were there others who survived this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO PUSELJA
utterances.text: Yes. There were some. And when I got up, I saw that there was nobody there; then I asked, "People, is there anyone else alive?"
